newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan's MOF seeks low defence budget growth - paper.
newsitem.headline: Japan's MOF seeks low defence budget growth - paper.

text.p: Japan's Finance Ministry will press for a one percent annual growth in defence spending next year, far below the 2.88 percent growth rate the defence agency has requested, a daily newspaper reported on Sunday.

Citing the need to retire some three trillion yen ($26.5 billion) in public debt, the finance ministry will push for an austere fiscal 1997 defence budget in negotiations later this month with the defence agency, the Yomiuri Shimbun daily quoted finance ministry sources as saying.
The defence agency had sought a 2.88 percent increase in its appropriations over the fiscal 1996 level of 4.85 trillion yen ($42.9 billion).
The 1997 fiscal year begins in April.

In budget negotiations set to be concluded by around December 20, the finance ministry would press the defence agency to cut spending on personnel expenses and meals, which account for 40 percent of defence outlays, the Yomiuri said.
Defence budget talks could bog down over the issue of how to fund the reconsolidation and relocation of U.S. military bases on the southern island of Okinawa.

U.S. and Japanese officials agreed on December 2 to cut back by one-fifth the land now taken up by the U.S. military on Okinawa, which hosts more than 75 percent of all U.S. military facilities in Japan.

Japan's defence budget rose 0.9 percent in fiscal 1994 and 0.86 percent in fiscal 1995. It was allowed to rise 2.58 percent in fiscal 1996 to cover payments for equipment contracted in previous years.
In a separate report, the business daily Nihon Keizai Shimbun said the overall fiscal 1997 national budget would grow between three and four percent to about 78 trillion yen ($690 billion).
